title: Royal Newfoundland Constabulary officer cleared of wrongdoing in fatal shooting of Omar Mohammed
subtitle: Serious Incident Response Team director says officer's actions were justified in circumstances
article: A Royal Newfoundland Constabulary officer who fatally shot a man in St. John's last June was justified and should not face a criminal charge, Newfoundland and Labrador's Serious Incident Response Team (SIRT) has concluded.

SIRT director Mike King released his report Tuesday, Dec. 12 into the shooting of 38-year-old Omar Mohammed at the provincial government income support office on Elizabeth Avenue June 12, and concluded the officer's use of force was necessary in the circumstances.
"(He) was protecting himself, his fellow officer and the employees working at Regatta Plaza," King wrote.
He did not name the officer nor the victim, but confirmed the latter as Mohammed in a media release shortly after the shooting.

King's report pieced together details of the incident through interviews with dozens of witnesses - 25 employees of Regatta Plaza, which houses the income support office; paramedics; police officers, including with the officer in question; and a friend of Mohammed.
Income support employees contacted police shortly before 10 a.m. to report Mohammed was there.
A week earlier, the RNC had issued a public request for help locating Mohammed, who was wanted on charges of violating court orders related to a 2022 conviction for sexual assaulting a woman.

Mohammed's longtime friend told SIRT Mohammed was originally from Darfur, Sudan, and had been staying with him after recently being evicted from his rental space. The friend said Mohammed had mentioned he was going to the income support office to pick up his rental cheque.
An employee at the office said she had told Mohammed a few days earlier she would not approve income support for him until he addressed the outstanding arrest warrant.

"When she recommended to (Mohammed) that he turn himself in, he called her racist and said he would return to her workplace the following day. He did not show up; however, staff at the (witness's) workplace were told not to let (Mohammed) in if he did," King wrote in his report.
Another employee mistakenly let Mohammed in on the morning of June 12.
By the time police arrived an hour after they were called, the office had been put on lockdown as Mohammed sat in the waiting room.

Several employees reported seeing Mohammed, who had been carrying a bag, lunge with his arm raised and swinging at a male officer; one described Mohammed attacking the officer with a hammer before the gunshot.
An RNC cadet who was on her first shift and training under the officer told SIRT that Mohammed took a hammer from a bag as they approached him, and refused to drop it.
When he threw the hammer at the male officer, the officer discharged his taser, but it had no effect.
Pepper spray wasn't an option, the cadet explained, since they were too close to Mohammed.

The cadet heard her colleague yell, "Drop the knife!" around the time of the gunshot, and told SIRT a knife had fallen from Mohammed's hand as he fell to the ground. Her colleague performed CPR until an ambulance arrived.
The cadet told investigators Mohammed would have stabbed the officer.
"(The cadet) felt (her colleague) had no choice but to do what he did," King wrote. "She described (Mohammed) as a 'big threat.' It seemed like he was waiting for the officers to arrive."
The officer who fired the shot said Mohammed had thrown a hammer at him, hitting him in the arm, and was coming toward him when he discharged his taser.
Mohammed backed him into a corner and was running at him, reaching for a knife at his side, when the officer fired the shot.
He told SIRT he was afraid Mohammed was going to seriously injure or kill him.
King determined the officer's fear was reasonable, since Mohammed "had displayed the intention and capability" to do it.

"(Mohammed) was a larger man than (the officer) and (the officer) was injured," King wrote. "At that point, (Mohammed) was literally backing (the officer) into a corner. In fact, (the officer) backed up until he could go no further before discharging his firearm. The threat was imminent and (the officer) had only seconds to react."

King indicated the investigation included a review of more than 500 clips of CCTV footage, which supported the witnesses' accounts, and the engagement of an independent use-of-force expert from outside the province.
The officer did not have any prior complaints on his RNC file related to excessive use of force, and was up to date on his use-of-force training.

King described Mohammed's previous contact with police, including an attempt to disarm an officer while being detained under the Mental Health Care and Treatment Act in 2017, altercations with prison and hospital staff in which he had bitten them, and two incidents in which he had punched police officers and pulled a knife on them.
His criminal record included convictions for assaulting police with a weapon, assault causing bodily harm, uttering threats, sexual assault and breaching court orders.

Mohammed's acquaintances, who expressed frustration in the week after his death with their failed attempts to confirm his identity with police, told CBC News he had been a child soldier in Sudan and struggled with his mental health as a result.
Mohammed's reported traumatic childhood was raised as a potential factor at his sentencing in provincial court last year, but he refused to discuss it.
